summary: This document adds an option to the Trivial File Transfer Protocol (TFTP) letting a client and server agree on a window size, so several data blocks can be sent before an acknowledgment is needed. This speeds up transfers over the otherwise lockstep protocol.

eli5.summary: TFTP sends one piece, then waits to hear back. This option lets it send several pieces before waiting, like handing over a stack of pages instead of one at a time.

questions: what is the tftp windowsize option
how to speed up tftp transfers
what is the maximum tftp windowsize
how does tftp windowsize error recovery work
subtitle: Lets a TFTP client and server agree to send several data blocks in a row before waiting for an acknowledgment.

tldr.problem: TFTP is a lockstep protocol: one data block, then a wait for its acknowledgment. That limits throughput on a LAN, which matters because TFTP is still heavily used for network boot and installation.
tldr.mechanism: A new windowsize option, negotiated with the TFTP option mechanism, sets how many consecutive blocks (1 to 65535) the sender transmits before it waits for an ACK of the last block in the window.
tldr.outcome: In the RFC's test, a 180 MByte transfer dropped from 257 seconds with a window of 1 to 35 seconds with a window of 64, with diminishing returns as the window grows.

facts.label: Error code if client refuses OACK

today: RFC 7440 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It extends TFTP through the option mechanism of RFC 2347.

sections.title: Why TFTP Needs a Window
sections.content:
The Trivial File Transfer Protocol (TFTP, RFC 1350) is a lockstep protocol: it sends one block and waits for its acknowledgment before sending the next. The RFC notes that TFTP is still widely used when computers boot or install over a network, including with EFI (Extensible Firmware Interface).

The blocksize option (RFC 2348) already helped. In practice, on Ethernet, blocks are no larger than 1468 bytes to avoid IP fragmentation. That is still not enough for big files such as the initial ramdisk of a Linux distribution or the PE images used in Microsoft network installations.

This RFC adds a negotiated option, built on the TFTP option extension (RFC 2347), that aims at transfer rates comparable to modern file transfer protocols.
sections.eli5: Waiting after every single page is slow, even if the pages are bigger. Sending a few pages at a time before waiting is a better fix.

sections.title: The Windowsize Option in a Request
sections.content:
The option rides in the normal Read Request (opcode 1) or Write Request (opcode 2). After the filename and mode come two more strings: windowsize (case insensitive) and the number of blocks as a base-10 ASCII string. Every field except the opcode is an ASCII string ending in a single NULL byte.

The value MUST be between 1 and 65535 blocks, inclusive. The RFC's example is a Read Request for the file foobar in octet mode with a windowsize of 16, using the default 512-byte block size.

If the server accepts the option, it answers with an Option Acknowledgment (OACK). The value in the OACK MUST be less than or equal to the client's value. The client then MUST either use that value or end the transfer with an ERROR packet with error code 8.
sections.eli5: The asker writes on the request slip how many pages it can take at once. The sender may say a smaller number, but never a bigger one.

sections.title: Traffic Flow and Error Recovery
sections.content:
The data sender (DSND) MUST send the agreed number of consecutive data blocks, then normally stop and wait. The data receiver (DRCV) MUST acknowledge the last block of the window to confirm that the whole window arrived.

Recovery is driven by the last good ACK:

  • If an expected ACK does not arrive in time, the last ACK received sets where the next window begins.
  • If the receiver sees a block out of sequence, it SHOULD send an ACK for the last block it received correctly. The sender SHOULD then start a new window based on that ACK.

A window shorter than the negotiated size is the final window. If the windowsize exceeds the data to send, the first window is the final one. Traffic with windowsize 1 MUST be equivalent to RFC 1350 traffic, and the final-packet rules are unchanged.
sections.eli5: If one page in the stack goes missing, the receiver says which page it last got properly, and the sender starts the next stack from there.

sections.title: Measured Speedups
sections.content:
The author tested a prototype on a lightly loaded Gigabit Ethernet between two laptops, in octet mode, with a fixed block size of 1456 bytes and a 180 MByte file. Times fell from 257 seconds with windowsize 1 to 131 (2), 76 (4), 54 (8), 42 (16), 38 (32) and 35 (64). The same transfer over a mapped SMB/CIFS drive took 23 seconds.

As a time reduction, that is 49% at windowsize 2, 70% at 4, 79% at 8, 84% at 16, 85% at 32 and 86% at 64. The RFC credits the gain to fewer synchronous acknowledgments.

Because returns diminish, operators SHOULD test various values and SHOULD be conservative. The best value depends on the network technology and topology.
sections.eli5: Sending a few pages at once made the job much faster, but sending a huge stack only helped a little more. A medium stack is the sweet spot.

sections.title: Congestion and Retry Limits
sections.content:
A big window is not in itself a threat to congestion signaling through drops, but the rate at which TFTP UDP datagrams are sent SHOULD follow the congestion control guidelines in Section 3.1 of RFC 5405.

Implementations SHOULD also set a maximum number of retransmission retries and abort the transfer after that, to prevent pathological retransmission. The RFC gives one example for 1 Gbit/s Ethernet with MTU 1500: windowsize 8, blksize 1456, 6 retransmission attempts per block or window, a 1 second timeout and a minimum inter-packet delay of 80 microseconds. Other values may suit other conditions.
sections.eli5: Even when you send a stack at once, you should not flood the road, and you should give up politely if the other side never answers.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
TFTP has no login or access control. Where authentication, access control, confidentiality or integrity checking are needed, those services must come from a layer above or below TFTP. Servers are often set up to serve only publicly readable files, and listing, deleting, renaming and writing are typically disallowed.

TFTP also has no protection against an on-path attacker, so windowsize values should be chosen according to what the sender, receiver and network can handle. The RFC states that this extension adds no security controls and poses no additional security risks.
sections.eli5: TFTP never checks who is asking, and this option does not change that. It also does not make things any riskier.
